articles.title: Holy shit holy shit holy shit holy shit: The magnitude of what’s now happening
articles.full_content:
HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT

I feel like my previous posts (and post titles), and podcasts, and talks, have failed to do full justice to the magnitude of what’s now happening, so I’m trying again.

Last night, we had friends and colleagues over for dinner. We were still trying to process OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s proofs of VP ≠ VNP—hot on the heels, obviously, of the Alpöge/Anthropic proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, which already feels like last week’s news. But then before dessert was served, we saw that OpenAI claims to prove that ω, the exponent of matrix multiplication, is exactly 9/4—a lower bound (!!), matching the upper bound that OpenAI proved in the great Mathocalypse drop of October 6.

There are two separate shocks here. The first shock is that we now, finally, know the right answer to this central mystery of algorithms going back to the late 1960s, when Volker Strassen first showed that ω<3 (he got ω≤log27) … and that the true answer is actually a rational number (!). But the even bigger shock is that the AI was able to prove any lower bound of the form ω>2. I never expected this challenge to be all that much easier than P ≠ NP.

Over the decades, I often heard colleagues express extreme confidence that ω=2, and I expressed skepticism whenever this came up—not because I had any strong argument for ω>2, but just because I saw that there was no strong argument for ω=2 either. So, I’m glad to have been vindicated about that!

But wait, there was more. During dessert, we saw another OpenAI release proving that the true number of linear gates needed to compute the Fourier Transform is N (log N)1/2+o(1). The upper bound here improves, not only over the O(N log N) that stood since the 1960s (i.e., the Fast Fourier Transform or FFT), but also over the O(N log0.9999999999999 N) (give or take some 9’s) that OpenAI published back in the October 6 Mathocalypse. Again, though, the real shock here is that there’s also a matching lower bound (!!). All these questions from the ancient days are now just getting … straight-up answered, rather than slowly illuminated with a drip-drip-drip of clues.

To give an idea of how much things have changed, the other day Yupan Liu put a preprint on the arXiv proving that QIP(2) = PSPACE—that is, quantum interactive protocols with only two messages have the full power of those with three, or any polynomial number. As recently as 2025, this would’ve considered been one of the top complexity results of the year, and the fact that Yupan had used AI to help achieve it would’ve been strange and wonderful. These days, I had to remind myself it had even happened, and the use of AI was so standard that it didn’t even raise an eyebrow.

It’s now obvious that we’ll be getting, not one-off solutions to this or that complexity question, but a whole new continent of mathematical truth, one that we’d previously only glimpsed through fog. Picture van Leeuwenhoek first training a microscope on pondwater, or Galileo first training his telescope on the stars. That might give you some idea of how our resolution into the complexity-theoretic universe, and the whole universe of mathematical truth beyond it, has now improved.

All through last night, as OpenAI and Anthropic uploaded more files to their GitHub repositories—because that’s what they’re doing now, they don’t even bother to issue press releases anymore, they just upload papers—my guests and I sat at the dinner table with phones out and a laptop, wondering which shoe was going to drop next. It was as though the clouds had parted above Mount Sinai, and we were waiting for the next sentence uttered by the Holy One Himself.

I now feel in my bones, for the first time ever, that a proof of P ≠ NP is not far.

For all I care, despise the AI companies for bulldozing our garden. Or love them for opening a new vista, or anything in between. Just please don’t deny what’s happening. Now that the companies have repeatedly shown that they can back up their claims with Lean certificates, don’t be a raging doofus who seizes on some triviality (e.g., a minor discrepancy between the Lean and informal proofs, or unused sections of the Lean proof) to pretend that dozens of great open problems of math and theoretical computer science are not, in fact, getting solved. Because they are getting solved. It might take us years to understand the solutions, but my working assumption by this point is that any proof that comes directly from OpenAI or Anthropic is correct barring information to the contrary.

I can’t possibly put the matter better than one of my friends on Facebook:

After years of crackpot “solutions” claiming Millennium Problems are solved, now that we have actual solutions, we have crackpot “refutations” claiming Millennium Problems are not solved. It is really poetic, in a way.

Along the way to so many lower bounds that we wondered whether ever we’d live to see, there will also, of course, be further shocking upper bounds: that is, ultimate barriers to lower bounds, also known as “algorithms.” And yes, some of those algorithms will break currently deployed cryptosystems.

Because people have been hounding me about it: yes, I’m virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells in that area. However, until I either see details or hear directly from someone at a lab, I feel much, much less confident about the specific nature of those bombshells. I do not wish to be responsible for spreading unverified rumors. And I worry that exact statements of what was done may have been mangled in a game of Telephone.

I also, crucially, don’t want the cryptography part of the story to overshadow the intellectual enormity of what’s happening. If, in these days of long-prophesied revelation and wonders and terrors, your main worry is your Bitcoin wallet, then go somewhere else for rumors about whether or not ECDSA is broken or whatever. I don’t have what you’re looking for here.

Let me be clear: for those of my readers who celebrate, I believe that tomorrow would be a superb Thanksgiving to spend some quality time with your kids and parents and siblings and old friends.

Right now—this past week—is very much like I would’ve always imagined the beginning of an AI singularity to look and feel like. I just hope we’ll get lucky, and it will “merely” be a singularity for our little corner of the world that involves hard math problems.

At some point at dinner last night, Dana had a sneezing fit. So I said to her, I hope it isn’t a swarm of nanobots that’s come to infect us! But if it is, then I hope it’s the friendly kind, the kind that will usher us all into an AI utopia.

Now, of course, another morning has dawned, and we’re still here. May we find a world where we and our children will be happy to live at the bottom of this rollercoaster. May we work to make it so.

articles.title: 1Password Security Incident
articles.full_content:
Back to blog

Update on a security incident involving 1Password’s backend systems. Customer vaults were not affected and all vault contents remain secure.

by 1Password

November 25, 2026 - 4 min

Related Categories

What happened

On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers. This data included customer names and email addresses, in addition to non-secret internal metadata about the account. At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker.

What information was affected

The attacker downloaded account records for a subset of our users. These records include:

  • Names and email addresses

  • Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times

  • Public keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security)

  • Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account)

  • Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery

  • Other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers)

The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system. Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. CI/CD contains infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work. We have triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed, and there is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security.

When we send an email to a customer to accept a provisioning invite to an account, or to accept recovery of their account, it contains a token. A provisioning invite is specifically used for our SCIM Bridge or Hosted Provisioning. During this incident there were a small number of users in this state, who have been specifically notified. This token is used to complete the invitation or recovery process, but only when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code sent to the user's registered email address. The token is not able to get access to the account by itself. In order to reduce the ability for a malicious third party to successfully guess the code, we’ve expanded the code from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric digits. This makes brute force guessing practically impossible.

What was not affected

  • Your vaults and the items in them

  • The keys that protect your vaults

    • 1Password does not store your account password or secret key

  • Account recovery keys

  • 1Password apps and browser extensions

What we’ve done

  • Disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access the attacker created.

  • Rotated or revoked all internal credentials which may have been exposed.

  • Lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure.

  • Tightened internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, and added new detections for this kind of attack.

  • Validated no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using any exposed account provisioning tokens.

  • Brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate our containment approaches and remediation efforts.

What you can do

  • Be cautious about phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts.

  • 1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser.

  • Keep your Secret Key and account password safe.

  • If you see something suspicious, tell us at support@1password.com.

Our commitment to you

You trust us with some of the most sensitive information you have. 1Password is designed so that a breach of our systems can’t expose your vault contents. Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers.

We are committed to transparency in the interests of our customers' security and the security of the broader industry, which is why we have published and maintained our Security Whitepaper since 2015.  We’ll keep this blog post current, and we’ll update it if we find anything that changes what we’ve said here.

articles.full_content:
The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.”

The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features

An email sent to freelance photographers says Photoshop’s latest update uses AI ‘in ways that may not be apparent.’

Adobe has spent the past few years filling Photoshop and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools. The November update cited by the NYT’s email adds several new AI features, including Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view, which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes.

It’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.”

In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads. NYT spokesperson Graham James confirmed the requirement in a statement to The Verge, which reiterated the policy outlined in the email.

It’s still not clear which specific Photoshop features the NYT is referring to. Adobe didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for more information.

Update, November 24th: Added confirmation from the NYT.

articles.full_content:
European IT spending set for 9.9% surge in 2027 amid AI-optimized server boom

Demand for high-performance compute and server costs will spur a surge in spending

Ross Kelly

Follow us

IT spending across Europe is expected to surge by 9.9% in 2027, according to new figures from Gartner, reaching a new high of $1.57 trillion.

Analysis by the firm projects enterprises will continue with AI infrastructure-related spending across the year. Investment in data center systems is expected to reach $167.6 billion, marking an increase on the $129 billion spent across 2026.

Infrastructure as a service (IaaS) spending will also surpass $82 billion, marking a 29.7% growth rate compared to the year prior.

Gartner said rising demand for high-performance compute means data center systems will remain Europe’s fastest-growing IT spending segment. Surging server prices are also a contributing factor here, however, with the analyst firm noting that costs could reach three-times those recorded in 2024.

All told, AI-optimized server spending across Europe is expected to total $79.7 billion, underlining a sharpened focus on the underlying infrastructure required to power AI build-outs.

“The build-out of the compute capacity needed for AI remains the largest infrastructure expansion in history, and AI-optimized servers constitute the core layer of the AI infrastructure,” said John-David Lovelock, distinguished VP analyst at Gartner.

The figures from Gartner come hot on the heels of global infrastructure spending projections, published on 12 November. AI infrastructure investment is expected to reach $2.4 trillion worldwide next year, with AI-optimized server spending set to increase from $527.6 billion in 2026 to $957.2 billion in 2027.

Software spending boom

Software-related investment is also projected to surge next year, according to Gartner, with spending closely linked to infrastructure build-outs.

Indeed, organizations are expected to spend roughly 38% of software budgets on infrastructure software as firms “prioritize the integration and scaling of AI across business processes”.

Spending on this front will top $385 billion, Gartner projects, marking 13.3% growth rate on 2026 levels.

Notably, the fastest software-related spending growth will be in AI models, with Gartner projecting a 50% growth rate in this domain.

“While software spending in Europe continues to reach double-digit growth rates, we expect a structural shift within the software segment affecting all regions,” said Lovelock.

“Today, European organizations are primarily purchasing isolated AI agents, but spending will shift toward agentic systems that can orchestrate workflow across the organization.”

“The near-term impact of cross-functional agentic AI will be modest, but the reallocation of software spending will place increasing pressure on traditional software and services markets,” Lovelock added.

articles.title: Do legacy systems wear out? (7 minute read)
articles.summary: This post examines how maintenance and vendor support shape the reliability of aging infrastructure. Hardware components deteriorate, but replacement parts, monitoring, and redundancy can keep an older platform operating reliably. Software presents a different challenge: changing workloads, missing patches, and the end of vendor support can make a functioning system increasingly risky. Upgrade or retire software before support ends, while maintaining the skills and parts needed to operate older
articles.full_content:
Legacy systems aren't the problem. Neglect is. Poor maintenance and outdated support turn dependable technology into a liability.

Dmitrijs Safrans

As I staggered into the computer room at three in the morning, I saw the look of fear on the operator’s face. The system was down again: not the first time this month. This legacy IBM mainframe was beginning to look like my stepfather’s car. I wondered: do legacy systems just wear out?

Old hardware

Let me tell you about my stepfather Tony and his car. The first time I sat in the passenger seat, I looked down and saw a steel plate welded to the floor, covering a hole that had rusted through. Water pipes poked up by the windscreen blowing hot air (when the heater worked), and as we sped along at an impressive 35 miles per hour, you could hardly talk from the sound of wind whistling through gaps. Not a comfortable driving experience. One more thing: it often broke down.

Experts talk about the ‘bathtub curve’ showing how things like computer equipment may fail early in their life from manufacturing defects, then have a stable period before the chance of failure increases with age. Tony’s car was an excellent demonstration of this, as old parts failed. This is what I faced as I entered the computer room.

The disk subsystem had failed, and everything else crashed as a result. At 3 am, this older disk subsystem looked like a bad idea.

Keep old hardware running

My Uncle Bill is around the same age as Tony and has a mint-condition Series 1 Land Rover. If you’re not a Land Rover fan, these were released in the late 1940s and 1950s: far older than Tony’s rust-bucket. But Bill’s car still hums along today.

Just like Bill’s Land Rover, older computing equipment is still in use: sometimes in critical areas. Germany’s train operator Deutsche Bahn made headlines in 2024 when it was found to rely on a Windows operating system not supported since 2001. In 2025, the FAA admitted to using equipment up to 50 years old.

Like Bill, the company I worked for kept this old hardware running by relying on support from an external vendor. This vendor performed regular maintenance and used hardware features to monitor its operation and predict failures. Although it didn’t predict my failure, the vendor provided 24/7 support. When the disk failed, the support engineer figured out the problem, found and obtained replacement parts, and installed them.

Vendors will often support hardware for years. For example, Apple stops supporting its devices 7 years after they are last sold. In my area of mainframes, IBM stops supporting its mainframe hardware 6-7 years after they are ‘end of marketing.’ Ideally, hardware is replaced before this time.

Rather than rely on external support, another option is to keep staff on site that can fix the hardware, together with spare hardware, or a cache of spare parts. In emergencies, like the FAA, they may resort to eBay.

Following Bill’s practices can keep older hardware running, and many do. But there was still an outage when my disk subsystem failed.

Critical systems like those in aircraft use redundancy to cope with this: multiple components doing the same job. If one fails, others keep running.

So, older hardware systems don’t wear out; individual components do. But what about software?

Software rot

Software isn’t made up of anything physical: there are no transistors to fail, no power supplies to catch fire. So, can a bunch of bytes wear out?

On 14-Oct-2025, Microsoft ended support of Windows 10. This doesn’t mean that Windows 10 stopped working on this date. Rather, Microsoft stopped providing fixes for Windows. However, StatCounter claims that 25% of all Windows users still use Windows 10, and some rely on even older versions.

As explained by the US Cyber Defense Agency, regularly updating software with patches and fixes is important to maximize security, with other possible benefits including performance improvements. In my mainframe world, knowing a vendor will guarantee their software works, and fix it if it doesn’t, is just as important. In fact, software support can be brilliant. One client had a critical system that failed to reboot in the middle of the night. The vendor had a fix shipped within hours.

As with hardware, vendors may end support. They may end support for a specific version like Windows 10, often providing an upgrade path to a new version. Or, like Broadcom, they may retire a product altogether. My clients should upgrade or retire software before support ends, though some don’t get there.

Bytes may not wear out, but software can face new problems not predicted when first developed. The Y2K problem is a great example: software storing the year as 2 digits in the 1990s would have problems come 2000. Vendors fixed supported products and guaranteed they would work after the year 2000. Note carefully the word ‘supported’: no one is fixing unsupported software.

Dates aren’t the only issue. Another client needed to double workloads to be processed by a suite of applications. Substantial changes were needed to their legacy COBOL software. Fortunately, they had staff supporting this software that could make these changes.

Some software may rely on other libraries, software, or standards. In May 2026, TLS versions 1.0 and 1.1 were deprecated. Software using these versions must be updated to provide acceptable security. Tony faced this when the government made retractable seat belts in cars mandatory. The solution for everyone is the same: those supporting the software must retrofit the required technology.

This doesn’t mean that all old software is ready to fail. In 1991 IBM released the most recent version of their Document Composition Facility (DCF) software. IBM still supports it, and I see clients happily using it today.

Storage

In my case, the disk subsystem had a storage medium failure: the disk crashed. Once the part was replaced, I restored data from backups on tape. But if disks can fail, can’t tape? Or any storage medium: flash drives, CDs?

The Library of Congress found that CDs last for over 30 years, a period matched by tape manufacturers like Fujifilm. But these figures assume the media is stored in correct conditions: Bill stores his Land Rover in a garage away from direct sunlight and dust.

Disk drives don’t last as long: Backblaze and SANDisk showed hard and solid-state disk drives failing from 3-10 years. Enterprise disk subsystems and cloud providers manage this with redundancy features. But anyone with an old single disk drive may be in trouble.

These figures will differ depending on the manufacturer, operating environment, and frequency of usage. Anyone subscribing to Tony’s maintenance ethos and buying cheaper or used parts will get what they pay for. But storage media needs the same attention as hardware and software: management, maintenance, and support.

Maintenance and care

The company I worked for looked after their systems well: hardware and software. They had support, installed updates, and stored storage media correctly. They followed Bill’s lead.

The computer systems were moved to a new data center, and the disks began to fail. The hardware vendor recommended replacing components for all disks, even though there was no immediate evidence they would fail. My company decided that the extra money and outages were not worth it. They leaned towards Tony’s methods and paid the price.

Legacy systems don’t wear out. Poorly maintained, managed or supported legacy systems do.

articles.title: I built an AI agent. It broke my assumptions about my own team (8 minute read)
articles.summary: CTO Matthew Finlayson describes building four versions of an agent to route customer issues to engineering teams. The project revealed that assignments depended on undocumented ownership rules, exceptions, and judgment that managers explained through reviewing real cases. He reports that their feedback helped improve routing accuracy from about 60% to 95%. articles.full_content:
Building an AI support agent revealed the hidden judgment behind everyday workflows and why successful automation requires validation and measurable results.

As a CTO, I’ve found that building AI automations gives me a better understanding of what I’m asking my team to do.

I’ve spent the past year building four iterations of an AI agent designed to route customer issues to the right engineering team. The first used Claude Code with an MCP connector to Jira. I’d hand it an issue and a prompt, and it would tell me who should look at it. For the second, I turned that workflow into an agent in n8n, a low-code framework. The third ran on Claude Managed Agents, Anthropic’s hosted agent platform. But I wanted it to have access to tools and data that the environment couldn’t reach. For the fourth, I rebuilt the agent on Google’s agent platform, where we run our production infrastructure. That gave it access to our codebase and issue tracker. I hadn’t anticipated how much data access would influence my platform of choice. As Grant Gross reports,data access and integration can be barriers to deploying agents.

Across each iteration, I kept asking whether the agent justified the work of building it. How often did it route an issue correctly? What did it cost to run? How much manual routing did it remove? Those questions gave me a way to evaluate the experiment.
The biggest surprise was discovering how much the routing process relied on knowledge our managers couldn’t fully articulate. Building the agent forced me to work through those decisions myself, giving me a better understanding of what I ask my team to do.

Here’s what I learned:

Understand the workflow before you automate

On paper, the workflow for my agent seemed ripe for automation. While our customer support team handles 90% of customer issues themselves, 10% involve product problems that require escalation to engineering. Routing those escalations was a bottleneck. Roughly 100 times a week, someone had to apply substantial domain knowledge to identify the right engineering manager.

Bernard Aceituno has similarly described successful agentic ticket-triage deployments that categorize issues and update the ticketing system. Given that my core problem was classification, I started with a simple mapping of product areas to engineering managers: this manager owns reports, this one owns the front end, this one owns administrative functions. But knowing the product area wasn’t always enough to route the ticket to the right team.

A reporting issue, for example, could have different causes. In some cases, an incorrect report indicated a front-end problem; in others, it indicated a data problem. Data ingestion belonged to one team unless the data came from an HRIS system, which another team handled. Even after the agent identified the right team, the person responsible could vary by request. My agent needed rules for both team ownership and individual assignment.

I couldn’t have asked any of the managers to write the complete set of routing rules upfront. But they could review a routing decision and say, “I would have sent it to this person for this reason.” Building the agent meant turning the group’s fragmented judgment into explicit rules.

Test whether the output is correct

The first version of the routing agent assigned only about 60% of issues correctly. It also made people up — hallucinating names, combining first and last names from different people. Engineering managers flagged incorrect assignments in Jira and explained which team or person should have received each ticket. I used those corrections to update the routing rules. Through that review process, the agent reached about 95% routing accuracy.

Checking the model’s behavior is another part of validation. Separate testing by our department showed how differently models can interpret the same restrictions. We tested OpenAI, Google and Anthropic models under rules that included a prohibition on giving employment recommendations. Gemini would go out of its way not to answer questions it felt crossed a line we had specified. Opus would get excessively creative trying to find ways to answer without violating the premise, while Sonnet followed the restriction more literally.

A new model release or even a new model family, such as a move from Claude Opus to GPT-6 or Gemini 4, can change those response patterns even when the surrounding tools and instructions stay the same. The same prompts, MCP connectors and guardrails can produce different tool-call behavior, formatting and refusals once the underlying model changes. That’s why validation needs to continue after deployment, particularly when the underlying model changes.

Decide where the automation should stop

The routing agent started with a specific job: given a problem description, what team owns that domain? And who’s the manager? But identifying the team raised other questions the agent might help answer.

I also built tools to ask: is this a regression — did a recent change cause it? Can I find the area of code where the problem lives? Do I know which developer touches that area? Together with routing, those capabilities made four tools that could be useful in sprint planning, product evaluations or other contexts. George Bezerra argues forchoosing among rules, machine learning, LLMs and agents based on the problem. Building those extra capabilities made me question how much machinery my original routing task needed.

The agent also explains its assignments in Jira: “I’m a bot, and I assigned this here for these reasons.” Anyone can put a thumbs down on it. The system captures that feedback, but it does not automatically learn from each correction. I stopped short of building that capability because each additional refinement saved less time. Managers redirect the remaining ~5% of incorrect assignments, just as they did before the agent existed.

Measure whether the system removes work

I started with a concrete metric to improve: how much time engineering managers were spending in the Jira project before and after the agent went live.

The agent now saves each of our seven engineering managers about 2 hours a week. Most issues now reach the right team immediately, reducing time to resolution. Another positive data point: when the agent broke for a week, several managers came to me, noticing the manual work had come back.

What surprised me was how small the actual operational cost of the agent is: pennies a month. That figure excludes the time I spent building and refining the agent, which matters when evaluating the total investment. But I had expected higher ongoing model costs.

Ongoing maintenance is another factor in ROI calculation. The routing rules reflect our current team structure, ownership boundaries and exceptions. When one team’s responsibilities changed, we had to adjust the routing rules.

Before building another agent, I need to ask: is this a fairly static workflow, or is the team or process going to change substantially? That changes the ROI calculation significantly.

Building an agent changed my process

I suspect by next year I’ll have multiple agents running to take over tasks for our team. Some I may purchase rather than build. Building this one gave me a better basis for evaluating either option.
Whether I build or buy, I’ll want to understand how an agent handles exceptions, adapts to workflow changes and justifies the effort required to maintain it. Low operating costs mean little if the system needs constant intervention to stay useful.

While the workflow required more investigation and iteration than I expected, the operating cost turned out to be much lower. Buying an agent raises some of the same questions. I can imagine agents that are durable through organizational changes. But I can also imagine a lot that aren’t. How are those delivered? As a service? As a toolkit I plug together? As a product that just works? These are the kinds of questions I’ll be asking.

I encourage other technology leaders to build an agent themselves. Documenting the workflow, investigating incorrect results and deciding whether another improvement is worth the effort gave me a clearer understanding of automation’s true cost and value — and of the work my team does every day.

articles.title: MCP servers can now ship skills, run tasks, and more with Claude (6 minute read)
articles.summary: Anthropic has launched Skills over MCP in public beta for Claude, allowing Model Context Protocol servers to publish specific workflows and guidance alongside their tools. Additionally, the company announced that Tasks and Elicitation features are now generally available to support long-running, interactive work and user sign-offs, with File Uploads rolling out soon.
articles.full_content:
MCP servers can now ship skills, run tasks, and more with Claude

Skills over MCP is now in public beta in Claude, so MCP servers can ship skills alongside their tools. We're also giving servers ways to handle longer, more interactive work with Claude: Tasks and Elicitation are now generally available, and File Uploads is rolling out soon.

Two years ago, Anthropic launched the Model Context Protocol (MCP) as a new standard for connecting AI agents to the systems where data lives. The spec has kept evolving to meet the connectivity needs of agents in production, and is becoming foundational for agentic messaging and orchestration.

With today’s updates, Claude can work with a server more like it works with another agent: learning from it, delegating to it, and exchanging input and files along the way.

Ship expertise alongside tools with Skills over MCP

Tool names and descriptions tell Claude what a server can do, but don't cover how to handle specific use cases. With Skills over MCP, servers can publish skills alongside their tools to help Claude take on longer, multi-step work. Claude loads a skill only when it's needed, keeping context use low. Skills update with the server, so developers can ship tools and guidance together and users have nothing separate to install.

Skills can cover best practices, step-by-step workflows, or even playbooks tailored to a user's account or organization. Using Skills over MCP:

  • Shopify helps Claude design and update a merchant's online store end to end.
  • HubSpot onboards customers and gets them set up in Claude.
  • Atlassian helps Claude draw on deep organizational context for insights and work analysis.
  • Carta will help Claude draft and issue equity from an uploaded document (coming soon).

Skills over MCP is in public beta in Claude and Claude Code, on by default for Pro, Max, and Ultra plans and available to Team plans once an admin enables it. Coming soon to Enterprise.

MCP servers can now take on long-running, interactive work with Claude

Agents in production are taking on longer, more consequential jobs. Servers can now support that work by running it in the background, checking in with users, and receiving files from Claude.

Hand off long-running work with Tasks. Tool calls used to have to finish before Claude could move on. With Tasks, servers can run operations that take time, or even full agent loops, while Claude keeps working and picks up the result when it's ready. Using Tasks, ZoomInfo runs deeper accounts and contact research that previously took several prompts.

Ask for input mid-call with Elicitation. Some actions need a user’s sign-off, like spending money or deleting data. With Elicitation, a server can pause to ask the user for input through a form or link, then continue where it left off. Using Elicitation:

  • Supabase confirms costs before creating a paid project and before running destructive SQL.
  • Railway asks before making potentially destructive changes, like removing a service.
  • GitHub has users enter a repository's name before an agent deletes it.

Tasks and Elicitation are now generally available in Claude and Claude Code for Pro, Max, and Ultra plans, and rolling out to Team and Enterprise organizations.

Send and receive files with File Uploads. Claude will be able to pass files to MCP servers, not just text. The File Uploads extension sends PDFs, spreadsheets, and images to a server without passing them through the context window.

File Uploads is rolling out soon in Claude and Claude Code to Pro, Max, Ultra, and eligible Team and Enterprise plans.

Add support to your plugins today

These features are part of the open MCP spec and its extensions, so a server that supports them works in any compatible client, not just Claude. To add support, see the docs for Skills over MCP, Tasks, Elicitation, and File Uploads.

Built on stronger foundations for connecting agents in production

Thanks to contributions from across the AI ecosystem, MCP now sees over 700 million monthly SDK downloads, and there are over 10,000 MCP connectors for Claude. We've worked with the MCP community to improve how MCP works in Claude. Over the past year, it has become:

  • More token efficient: Tool search loads tool definitions only when needed, which can cut the context they use by over 85% in multi-server setups.
  • Easier to scale: The latest MCP spec is stateless and supported across Claude products, making it easier to build servers and maintain their reliability as they grow.
  • Simpler to authorize: The Enterprise Managed Auth extension lets admins authorize supported servers once, so users connect automatically.
  • More interactive: The MCP Apps extension brings full interfaces into Claude, beside the conversation or full screen.

Together, these improvements make MCP easier to build on and adopt, and give the standard a strong base to continue evolving for the needs of agents in production.

Thank you to the MCP community

MCP is an open standard, hosted by the Agentic AI Foundation and shaped by the people who build on it. Two years of progress came from the maintainers, contributors, and developers who wrote the spec, built the SDKs, shipped servers, and added client support. Thank you for making MCP what it is today.
